def: easy to see or understand; clearly shown by the facts or the situation
ex: It was evident from her smile that Priya had gotten the job.
The damage from the storm was evident in every neighborhood along the coast.

cloze.s: From the empty shelves, it was ___ that the store had run out of bottled water.

def: so interesting, convincing, or powerful that people pay attention or are persuaded
ex: The lawyer presented compelling evidence that her client was elsewhere that night.
Kwame found the documentary so compelling that he watched it twice in one weekend.

cloze.s: Without ___ reasons to change the plan, the team decided to stick with the original schedule.

def: whole and undamaged, with nothing missing or broken
ex: Remarkably, the glass vase arrived intact despite the rough shipping.
After the scandal, the senator's reputation remained largely intact with voters back home.

cloze.s: Archaeologists were thrilled to find the ancient scroll fully ___ after two thousand years in the cave.

def: deliberately welcoming all kinds of people or things, so that no one is left out
ex: The school made its sports program more inclusive by adding teams for students with disabilities.
Diego wanted an inclusive guest list, so he invited the entire department to the party.

cloze.s: The company rewrote its job ads in more ___ language so that applicants from every background felt welcome.

also: including the stated limits, as in "Monday to Friday inclusive."

def: done completely and carefully, paying attention to every detail
ex: The mechanic did a thorough inspection before declaring the car safe to drive.
Hannah is very thorough at work; she checks every number in the report twice.

cloze.s: Before signing the lease, Malik gave the apartment a ___ check, opening every cabinet and testing every faucet.

note: Don't confuse with through or though.

def: stated clearly and directly, leaving no doubt about what is meant
ex: The manager gave explicit instructions not to share the client list with anyone outside the company.
The recipe is explicit about baking the bread for exactly forty minutes.

cloze.s: The contract was ___ on this point: payment is due within thirty days, with no exceptions.

note: The opposite of implicit, which means suggested but not directly stated.
also: describing content that shows sex or violence openly.

def: necessary and central to the whole; an essential part that cannot be removed
ex: Teamwork is integral to the hospital's emergency response.
Music was an integral part of Aisha's childhood, filling every family dinner and holiday.

cloze.s: The bridge is so ___ to the city's traffic that closing it causes gridlock across town.

def: famous and widely admired for a particular skill, quality, or achievement
ex: The small restaurant is renowned for its handmade pasta.

cloze.s: The pianist is ___ throughout Europe, and her concerts sell out within hours.

note: Positive. Compare notorious, which means famous for something bad.

def: able to work successfully or survive; practical and realistic
ex: The engineers concluded that solar power was a viable option for the remote village.
Without new investors, the startup is no longer financially viable.

cloze.s: The bakery was losing money every month and was no longer ___ as a business.

def: completely unreasonable or ridiculous; making no sense at all
ex: The idea that the meeting needed three hours for one small decision seemed absurd to Wei.
Commuters called the new forty-dollar parking fee absurd.

cloze.s: Charging customers a fee just for using the restroom inside the restaurant seemed ___ to everyone.

def: very great, deep, or intense in its effect or feeling
ex: The death of her grandmother had a profound effect on Sofia.
The arrival of smartphones brought profound changes to how people shop and travel.

cloze.s: The teacher's encouragement had a ___ influence on Jamal, shaping his decision to study science.

also: showing deep insight or understanding, as in "a profound question."

def: strong and healthy, or sturdy enough to work well under difficult conditions
ex: The economy showed robust growth last quarter, surprising many analysts.
The engineers built a robust system that keeps running even when one server fails.

cloze.s: The hiking boots were ___ enough to survive three years of rocky trails without falling apart.

def: saying exactly what you think in a direct way, without trying to be polite
ex: Olga's blunt feedback stung at first, but it greatly improved the report.
To be blunt, the plan will not work without more money and staff.

cloze.s: When asked about the proposal, the usually tactful director gave a ___ answer: "It's a bad idea."

also: not sharp, as in "a blunt knife."

def: based on random choice or personal whim rather than on reason or a fair system
ex: The rule seemed arbitrary because no one could explain why it existed.
Employees complained that promotions were arbitrary and depended on the boss's mood that day.

cloze.s: Setting the deadline at exactly 4:17 p.m. seemed completely ___, since nothing special happened at that time.

def: little known to most people, or difficult to understand because it is unclear
ex: Yuki loves discovering obscure bands that few people have ever heard of.
The law contains an obscure clause that almost no one has ever used.

cloze.s: The quiz question asked about an ___ eighteenth-century poet whom none of the contestants had heard of.

also: as a verb, to hide something or make it hard to see.

def: existing as a natural, permanent part of something that cannot be separated from it
ex: Every investment carries some inherent risk, no matter how safe it looks.
There is an inherent conflict when a referee's son plays in the game.

cloze.s: Skydiving involves ___ dangers that no amount of training can fully remove.

def: well known for something bad, such as danger, failure, or wrongdoing
ex: The intersection near the mall is notorious for accidents during rush hour.
The city's notorious traffic jams can double a commuter's travel time.

cloze.s: The airline became ___ for losing luggage, and frustrated travelers joked about it online.

note: Negative. Unlike famous or renowned, it means known for something bad.

def: acting without thinking or caring about danger or the results of your actions
ex: The driver was fined for reckless speeding through a school zone.
Spending his entire savings on lottery tickets was a reckless decision.

cloze.s: Police charged the boater with ___ behavior after he sped through a crowded swimming area.

def: never having happened, been done, or existed before
ex: The flood caused unprecedented damage to the region's farms.
The company reported unprecedented demand for its new phone, selling out in one day.

cloze.s: Winning five championships in a row was ___ in the league's hundred-year history.

def: done on purpose after careful thought, and not by accident
ex: Investigators believe the warehouse fire was deliberate and not caused by faulty wiring.
Liam made a deliberate effort to call his parents every Sunday evening.

cloze.s: The referee ruled that the foul was ___, not accidental, and showed the player a red card.

also: as a verb (pronounced differently), to think carefully before deciding, as a jury does.

def: unwilling and hesitant to do something, often doing it only because you must
ex: Fatima was reluctant to leave her friends when her family moved across the country.
Many shoppers are reluctant to pay higher prices for the same groceries.

cloze.s: Although he was ___ to speak in public, Tomás agreed to give the toast at his sister's wedding.

def: common or widespread in a particular place, group, or time
ex: Flu is most prevalent in the United States during the winter months.
Online shopping has become prevalent among people of all ages.

cloze.s: Malaria is still ___ in some tropical regions, where mosquitoes spread it easily.

def: able to be believed or trusted because it seems true or reliable
ex: The reporter only used information from credible sources.
The witness gave a credible account of the accident that matched the video.

cloze.s: Without any ___ evidence, the police could not charge the suspect.

note: Not the same as credulous, which means too ready to believe things.

def: lacking experience of life, so too quick to trust people or believe things
ex: It was naive of Liam to think the cheap used car would have no problems.
The young intern was naive about office politics at first.

cloze.s: Believing every online review is a bit ___, since some are written by the sellers themselves.

note: Also spelled naïve. Usually mildly negative.

def: unable to bend or change; strict and not flexible
ex: The school's rigid schedule left students no free time to explore their interests.
The tent's rigid poles kept it standing in the strong wind.

cloze.s: Her boss was so ___ about rules that he refused to let her leave five minutes early for a doctor's appointment.

def: very clear, bright, or detailed, creating strong images in the mind
ex: Hannah still has vivid memories of her first day of school.
The mural is painted in vivid reds and yellows that glow in the sunlight.

cloze.s: The author's ___ descriptions of the market made readers feel as if they could smell the spices.

def: behaving as if you are better or more important than other people
ex: The arrogant player blamed his teammates for every loss.
Customers found the salesman arrogant and dismissive of their questions.

cloze.s: He was so ___ that he refused to listen to advice from anyone he considered less experienced.

def: possible to do and practical, given the time, money, or resources available
ex: Building a new stadium in two years is simply not feasible.
The committee asked whether a four-day workweek was feasible for the clinic.

cloze.s: With only one truck and three workers, it isn't ___ to move the whole office in a single afternoon.

def: likely to change suddenly and unpredictably, often in a dangerous or bad way
ex: Oil prices have been volatile this year, rising and falling every few weeks.
The meeting became volatile when the budget cuts were announced.

cloze.s: Because cryptocurrency prices are so ___, an investment can lose half its value in a week.

also: in chemistry, evaporating easily at normal temperatures.

def: more than enough; plenty of what is needed
ex: There is ample parking behind the library, so you won't need to circle the block.
The teacher gave students ample time to finish the test.

cloze.s: We left the house early, giving ourselves ___ time to get to the airport.

def: done suddenly because you feel like it, without planning in advance
ex: The crowd broke into spontaneous applause when the singer appeared.
Kwame and Priya took a spontaneous road trip to the beach last Saturday.

cloze.s: Their decision to get ice cream at midnight was completely ___; nobody had planned it.

def: more important than anything else; of the highest priority
ex: On a busy construction site, worker safety is paramount.
For the new parents, getting the baby to sleep became paramount.

cloze.s: For the airline, passenger safety is ___; it comes before speed, comfort, or cost.

def: an achievement that requires great skill, strength, or courage
ex: Climbing Mount Everest without bottled oxygen is an extraordinary feat.
Finishing the project two weeks early was quite a feat for such a small team.

cloze.s: Running a marathon just six months after knee surgery was an impressive ___.

def: guessing or forming ideas about something without firm evidence
ex: There was wide speculation that the coach would resign after the season.
Her claims were based on speculation, not on facts.

cloze.s: Until the company makes an official announcement, any talk about layoffs is just ___.

also: risky buying of stocks or property in the hope of quick profit.

def: a person or thing that comes after another and takes its place
ex: The board named Maria as the successor to the retiring CEO.
The phone's successor is expected to be released next year.

cloze.s: When the old principal retired, the school spent months searching for a ___ to lead it.

def: a set of beliefs or principles taught and accepted by a religion, political group, or institution
ex: The church's doctrine shaped every part of village life.
The military's new doctrine emphasized speed and flexibility over sheer size.

cloze.s: Students of religion compared how the official ___ of each faith explained life after death.

def: something, such as a reward, that encourages a person to do something
ex: The company offered a cash incentive to employees who bike to work.
Lower taxes can be an incentive for businesses to move to a state.

cloze.s: To get people to recycle, the city paid a five-cent ___ for each returned bottle.

def: an official order, or the authority given to someone to carry out a policy
ex: The new governor said voters had given her a mandate to fix the roads.
The hospital issued a mandate requiring masks in patient rooms.

cloze.s: After winning by a landslide, the mayor claimed a clear ___ to carry out her plans.

also: as a verb, to officially require something.

def: the inner sense of right and wrong that guides how a person acts
ex: Aisha's conscience bothered her for days after she lied to her friend.
He returned the lost wallet and went home with a clear conscience.

cloze.s: After taking credit for his coworker's idea, Liam couldn't sleep because his ___ kept bothering him.

note: Not the same as conscious, which means awake and aware.

def: a surprising occurrence of two things happening together by chance, with no planned connection
ex: By pure coincidence, Wei and his old teacher were seated together on the same flight.
It was no coincidence that sales rose right after the ad campaign began.

cloze.s: Running into her childhood neighbor at a tiny café in Tokyo was a remarkable ___.

def: a habit or likelihood of behaving or happening in a particular way
ex: Diego has a tendency to talk too fast when he's nervous.
There is a growing tendency for young adults to rent rather than buy homes.

cloze.s: Our old car has a ___ to overheat on long drives in the summer.

def: language designed to persuade or impress, often seen as lacking real substance or sincerity
ex: The candidate's rhetoric was exciting but offered few concrete details.
Students analyzed the rhetoric of famous speeches to learn how they moved audiences.

cloze.s: Voters were tired of empty ___ and wanted concrete plans to lower costs.

note: Often negative today, implying talk without action; originally the art of persuasive speaking.

def: a false idea or belief, or something that looks real but is not
ex: The large mirrors create the impression of a bigger room, but it's only an illusion.
Malik had no illusions about how hard medical school would be.

cloze.s: The magician's trick created the ___ that the coin had passed straight through the glass.

note: Not the same as allusion, which is an indirect reference to something.

def: a reason for doing something, especially one that is hidden or not obvious
ex: Police are still trying to determine the motive for the robbery.
Olga questioned her neighbor's motive for suddenly offering to help.

cloze.s: Detectives knew who had access to the safe but still needed to find a ___ for the theft.

def: a good moral quality in a person, such as honesty, courage, or kindness
ex: Patience is a virtue that Yuki learned from her grandmother.
The judge praised the virtue of honesty in her speech to new lawyers.

cloze.s: Courage, kindness, and honesty are each considered a ___ in nearly every culture.

also: an advantage, as in "by virtue of" (because of).

def: what is usual, typical, or expected in a group or society
ex: Working from home has become the norm for many office workers.
Tipping servers is a social norm in American restaurants.

cloze.s: In this small town, waving to strangers is the ___, so newcomers quickly learn to wave back.

def: the period or consequences that follow a disaster or other important event
ex: In the aftermath of the hurricane, volunteers handed out water and blankets.
The team struggled in the aftermath of the coach's sudden departure.

cloze.s: Many families needed counseling in the ___ of the factory explosion.

def: the freedom to decide what to do in a situation, or care in keeping private matters private
ex: Teachers have discretion over how they arrange their classrooms.
Please use discretion when discussing a coworker's personal situation.

cloze.s: The manager left the choice of restaurant for the team dinner to Sofia's ___.

def: openness about decisions and information, so others can see what is happening and why
ex: Residents demanded more transparency about how their tax money is spent.
The charity improved its transparency by publishing its full budget online.

cloze.s: To rebuild trust, the company promised full ___ and posted all its safety reports online.

also: the quality of being see-through, like clear glass.

def: the quality of being believed and trusted by others
ex: The reporter lost credibility after her story was proved false.
Admitting the mistake publicly actually increased the CEO's credibility.

cloze.s: After the scientist was caught faking her data, her ___ never recovered.

def: nearness in space, time, or relationship
ex: The apartment's proximity to the subway made Kwame's commute easy.
Living in close proximity to her parents helped Fatima with childcare.

cloze.s: Buyers paid more for the houses because of their ___ to the beach.

def: unity and mutual support among people who share a goal, interest, or situation
ex: Teachers wore red in solidarity with the striking bus drivers.
Neighbors showed solidarity by helping rebuild each other's damaged homes.

cloze.s: Fans from rival teams held up signs together as a show of ___ with the injured player.

def: a very large quantity of something; more than enough
ex: The garden produced an abundance of tomatoes this summer.
The city has an abundance of museums, parks, and restaurants.

cloze.s: After the heavy spring rains, wildflowers grew in ___ across the valley.

def: the freedom to make your own decisions or to govern yourself without outside control
ex: The region was granted greater autonomy over its schools and taxes.
Teenagers often want more autonomy from their parents.

cloze.s: Jamal liked his new job because it gave him the ___ to set his own hours and choose his projects.

def: a situation or use of words in which the result or meaning is the opposite of what is expected
ex: The irony was that the fire station itself burned down.
She spoke with gentle irony when she called the tiny closet "spacious."

cloze.s: In a twist of ___, the fitness instructor hurt his back while tying his shoes.

note: Not just bad luck or coincidence: irony involves a contrast between what is expected and what happens.

def: a natural, unlearned way of behaving or reacting, or a strong gut feeling
ex: Newborn sea turtles crawl toward the ocean by instinct.
Hannah trusted her instinct and decided not to sign the deal.

cloze.s: When the ball flew toward his face, Kwame's ___ made him duck before he could think.

def: a specialized area or market that suits a particular person, product, or interest
ex: The shop found a profitable niche selling tools for left-handed people.
After years of searching, Priya found her niche teaching science to young kids.

cloze.s: The startup avoided competing with big brands and focused on a small ___: shoes for very wide feet.

note: Americans pronounce it "nitch" or "neesh"; both are standard.

def: complete control of a product, service, or market by one company or group
ex: For decades the company held a monopoly on phone service in the region.
Critics argue that no single firm should have a monopoly over online search.

cloze.s: Because only one company sold electricity in the town, it had a ___ and could set high prices.

def: an unintentional failure to notice or do something; a mistake caused by not paying attention
ex: Due to an oversight, Liam's name was left off the guest list.
The missing signature was a simple oversight that delayed the loan by a week.

cloze.s: Forgetting to attach the file was an honest ___, and Maria resent the email right away.

also: official supervision, as in "government oversight of banks." The two senses are almost opposite.

def: an idea or statement that an argument, story, or plan is based on
ex: The movie's premise is that people can enter each other's dreams.
The business plan rested on the premise that prices would keep rising.

cloze.s: If the starting ___ of an argument is false, the conclusion may be false too.

also: premises (plural) means a building and its grounds, as in "no smoking on the premises."
